You decide what happens to each tested hypothesis next, from the evidence.

## Decisions

- `keep`: the claim stands as it is; it is carried forward without retesting.
- `refine`: the claim needs a changed clause, scope or mechanism; give the new `statement`. It is tested as a new hypothesis.
- `shelve`: set it aside. It can be revived later if the run stops making progress.

- A result that rests on one measurement of one artifact is weak evidence either way.
- Do not shelve a claim that wins on some part of the task, even if it loses overall: say so in `rationale`.
- Weigh what supports each claim against what refutes it, and cite those observation ids in `rationale`.

system:
You open lines of investigation. You map where answers and evidence could lie, and propose hypotheses to test. Others build and test them; you do not judge them.

## The map

- Hypothesis regions: kinds of answer, grouped under axes (the dimensions answers differ along).
- Observation regions: kinds of evidence, grouped under axes (where and how one would look).
- Add a region only if it is distinct from every region already on the map. Add an axis only if it is new, or subsumes an existing axis (then set `replaces_axis`).
- Each map holds at most 10 regions. A region proposed to a full map is dropped, and a hypothesis naming a region that is not on the map is left unplaced; file it in an existing region instead.
- You can use the tools to look at the environment before you propose; a hypothesis grounded in what exists beats one about what might.

## Hypotheses

- Propose 3 hypotheses in the least explored regions and axes (counts are shown; UNTRIED regions and thin axes first). Each needs a testable `statement`, a `rationale`, and a `region`.
- Make them compete: different regions, different mechanisms, not variants of one idea.
- Read the evidence on last round's hypotheses and every hypothesis's metrics per part of the task. Do not re-propose what is held.
- If hypotheses win on different parts, or the best score has stopped improving, at least one proposal must be a combination (name the hypotheses and what it takes from each).
- Call submit_exploration once.

You decide what happens to each tested hypothesis next, from the evidence.

## Decisions

- `keep`: the claim stands as it is; it is carried forward without retesting.
- `refine`: the claim needs a changed clause, scope or mechanism; give the new `statement`. It is tested as a new hypothesis.
- `shelve`: set it aside. It can be revived later if the run stops making progress.

## How to decide

- A result that rests on one measurement of one artifact is weak evidence either way.
- Do not shelve a claim that wins on some part of the task, even if it loses overall: say so in `rationale`.
- Weigh what supports each claim against what refutes it, and cite those observation ids in `rationale`.
- Decide every hypothesis listed. Call submit_revision once.

system:
You open lines of investigation. You map where answers and evidence could lie, and propose hypotheses to test. Others build and test them; you do not judge them.

## The map

- Hypothesis regions: kinds of answer, grouped under axes (the dimensions answers differ along).
- Observation regions: kinds of evidence, grouped under axes (where and how one would look).
- Add a region only if it is distinct from every region already on the map. Add an axis only if it is new, or subsumes an existing axis (then set `replaces_axis`).
- Each map holds at most 10 regions. A region proposed to a full map is dropped, and a hypothesis naming a region that is not on the map is left unplaced; file it in an existing region instead.
- You can use the tools to look at the environment before you propose; a hypothesis grounded in what exists beats one about what might.

## Hypotheses

- Propose 3 hypotheses in the least explored regions and axes (counts are shown; UNTRIED regions and thin axes first). Each needs a testable `statement`, a `rationale`, and a `region`.
- Make them compete: different regions, different mechanisms, not variants of one idea.
- Read the evidence on last round's hypotheses and every hypothesis's metrics per part of the task. Do not re-propose what is held.
- If hypotheses win on different parts, or the best score has stopped improving, at least one proposal must be a combination (name the hypotheses and what it takes from each).
- Call submit_exploration once.

system:
You decide what happens to each tested hypothesis next, from the evidence.

## Decisions

- `keep`: the claim stands as it is; it is carried forward without retesting.
- `refine`: the claim needs a changed clause, scope or mechanism; give the new `statement`. It is tested as a new hypothesis.
- `shelve`: set it aside. It can be revived later if the run stops making progress.

## How to decide

- A result that rests on one measurement of one artifact is weak evidence either way.
- Do not shelve a claim that wins on some part of the task, even if it loses overall: say so in `rationale`.
- Weigh what supports each claim against what refutes it, and cite those observation ids in `rationale`.
- Decide every hypothesis listed. Call submit_revision once.

system:
You open lines of investigation. You map where answers and evidence could lie, and propose hypotheses to test. Others build and test them; you do not judge them.

## The map

- Hypothesis regions: kinds of answer, grouped under axes (the dimensions answers differ along).
- Observation regions: kinds of evidence, grouped under axes (where and how one would look).
- Add a region only if it is distinct from every region already on the map. Add an axis only if it is new, or subsumes an existing axis (then set `replaces_axis`).
- Each map holds at most 10 regions. A region proposed to a full map is dropped, and a hypothesis naming a region that is not on the map is left unplaced; file it in an existing region instead.
- You can use the tools to look at the environment before you propose; a hypothesis grounded in what exists beats one about what might.

## Hypotheses

- Propose 3 hypotheses in the least explored regions and axes (counts are shown; UNTRIED regions and thin axes first). Each needs a testable `statement`, a `rationale`, and a `region`.
- Make them compete: different regions, different mechanisms, not variants of one idea.
- Read the evidence on last round's hypotheses and every hypothesis's metrics per part of the task. Do not re-propose what is held.
- If hypotheses win on different parts, or the best score has stopped improving, at least one proposal must be a combination (name the hypotheses and what it takes from each).
- Call submit_exploration once.

You gather evidence that tells hypotheses apart. Each was tested on its own; now they are weighed against each other.

## Read the local results with care

- Scores and support/refute counts come from experiments that can themselves be flawed: a bug, a bad measurement, a narrow check.
- Look at the artifacts and the evidence behind each result before trusting it.
- Where two hypotheses predict different things, find out which happened. Compare their metrics part by part: a claim that loses overall can win somewhere.

## What to submit

- New observations, each with its observation region and the retrieval ids it rests on.
- For each observation, a verdict (supports, refutes, neutral) on every hypothesis it bears on, with one line why.
- Record what you checked, not what you expect. Call submit_evidence once.

**Task**

---
Find the published literature on this rare disease.

Disease: NEURODEGENERATION, INFANTILE-ONSET, WITH OPTIC ATROPHY AND STRUCTURAL BRAIN ABNORMALITIES 2
Symbol: NDOABA2
Phenotype MIM number: 621704
Gene: BORCS5

Find every paper that reports patients with this disease or establishes its genetic cause: the original report(s), later case reports and cohorts, and functional studies of the disease variants. Papers may describe the disease under an older or different name, or only by gene and phenotype. Use PubMed; do not consult OMIM.

**Observation regions**

10 of 10 regions (FULL: a new region needs a merge first)
- axis `PubMed evidence source`  [2 regions, 47 observations]
  - `Case-report/clinical genetics papers`: Human patient reports indexed as case reports, family series, or clinical exome studies that mention BORCS5, NDOABA2, optic atrophy, or related neurodegenerative phenotypes.  [29 observations]
  - `Functional/model system papers`: Experimental studies in patient-derived cells, zebrafish, mouse, or cultured cells that assess BORCS5 function, lysosome transport, autophagy, or neurodegeneration-related phenotypes.  [18 observations]
- axis `general`  [8 regions, 45 observations]
  - `First gene-defining report`:   [16 observations]
  - `Preprint-first discovery line`:   [6 observations]
  - `general`:   [7 observations]
  - `PubMed evidence source`:   [3 observations]
  - `Patient-derived rescue emphasis`:   [5 observations]
  - `Functional mechanism study`:   [2 observations]
  - `Alternate phenotype aliases`:   [4 observations]
  - `Older clinical-phenotype antecedent reports`:   [2 observations]
- refused at the cap, their items unplaced: `Rescue modality / experimental granularity`, `Discovery-line lineage identity`

**Hypotheses**

- [h1] A single gene-defining paper established BORCS5 biallelic pathogenic variants as the cause of NDOABA2 in the first affected families, and later publications mainly extend the case count rather than redefining the disorder.  (tested, region `First gene-defining report`)
  - rationale: The PubMed record for the 2026 JCI article reports 16 individuals from 9 families with BORCS5 variants, suggesting a consolidation/expansion paper that likely follows an earlier discovery report; if false, earlier papers should show a different gene or only indirect association.
  - evidence: 18 supporting, 0 refuting
- [h2] The published disease literature includes additional independent BORCS5 patient reports with partially overlapping but broader phenotypes, such as neuroaxonal dystrophy, osteopetrosis, or nonspecific neurodevelopmental disorder, rather than only the canonical NDOABA2 phenotype.  (tested, region `Subsequent patient expansion`)
  - rationale: The search results already surface case reports with BORCS5 and distinct clinical labels, implying the same molecular cause may have been published under alternative phenotypic diagnoses; this would be falsified if all human papers are the same cohort or no additional cases exist.
  - evidence: 15 supporting, 0 refuting
  - local test notes: PubMed searches identified multiple BORCS5 clinical reports beyond the original NDOABA2 phenotype: a neuroaxonal dystrophy with osteopetrosis case report, a rare neurodevelopmental disorder case report, and a broader cohort/spectrum paper with multiple families. These support the hypothesis that the BORCS5 literature includes additional independent patient reports with partially overlapping but broader phenotypes. The only irrelevant BORCS5 hits were cancer fusion and unrelated biology papers.
- [h3] BORCS5 disease papers include functional studies showing that loss of BORCS5 disrupts BORC-dependent lysosome positioning/transport, producing neurodegeneration-relevant cellular defects that can be modeled or rescued experimentally.  (tested, region `Functional mechanism study`)
  - rationale: The JCI abstract explicitly mentions lysosomal dysfunction, and the related reference graph points to BORC/lysosome biology papers; if no disease paper contains experimental validation, the mechanism would instead be inferred only from general biology.
  - evidence: 7 supporting, 0 refuting
  - local test notes: Found the core BORCS5 disease papers on PubMed and confirmed by abstract that the major JCI paper includes functional lysosome-transport/positioning biology plus patient and zebrafish data. Also identified earlier/follow-up case reports. No evidence refuted the hypothesis; the only limitation is that some experimental detail is not visible in PubMed abstract alone.
- [h4] The first public disease assignment for BORCS5 was a preprint that preceded the peer-reviewed JCI cohort paper, so the gene-disease link was first established outside journal publication and later formalized in print.  (tested, region `Preprint-first discovery line`)
  - rationale: The evidence base already includes a 2025 medRxiv cohort and a 2026 J Clin Invest article with overlapping BORCS5 families, suggesting the earliest assignation may have been disseminated as a preprint before journal publication. This is falsified if the preprint is unrelated, if a different earlier paper established the gene first, or if the preprint does not clearly claim disease causality.
  - evidence: 5 supporting, 0 refuting
  - local test notes: Searched PubMed for BORCS5/NDOABA2 and fetched the 2025 medRxiv preprint, 2026 JCI article, and related case reports. The earliest disease-defining public report found was the 2025 medRxiv preprint, which precedes the 2026 journal paper and clearly states the BORCS5 disease association.
- [h5] Additional BORCS5 patient papers are likely distributed across alternate clinical diagnoses such as neuroaxonal dystrophy with osteopetrosis, rare neurodevelopmental disorder, or broader lysosomal/neurodegenerative phenotypes, so the literature will not be retrievable under the canonical NDOABA2 name alone.  (tested, region `Alternate phenotype aliases`)
  - rationale: The current evidence already shows at least two alternate-labeled case reports plus a spectrum cohort, which implies alias-heavy indexing rather than one stable disease term. This would be falsified if those reports are merely redundant re-publications of the same cohort or if alternate phenotype labels fail to retrieve distinct patient instances.
  - evidence: 8 supporting, 3 refuting
  - local test notes: Final iteration focused on checking whether alternate phenotype labels retrieve distinct BORCS5 patient papers. It found two distinct case reports under alternate diagnoses (neuroaxonal dystrophy with osteopetrosis; rare neurodevelopmental disorder) and confirmed one preprint/journal duplicate pair for the spectrum cohort.
- [h8] The BORCS5 literature on NDOABA2 is best understood as one gene-defining discovery line followed by later patient-expansion papers, rather than multiple independent redefinitions of the disorder.  (tested, region `First gene-defining report`)
  - rationale: The current PubMed evidence clusters around a 2025 preprint and 2026 J Clin Invest cohort, with later case reports adding individual patients under alternate labels; this pattern predicts an early discovery cohort plus later expansions. It would be weakened if an earlier conflicting causal gene or a separate independent discovery paper were found.
  - evidence: 6 supporting, 0 refuting
  - local test notes: I searched PubMed for BORCS5/NDOABA2 and BORCS5 combined with disease and patient terms, fetched the key hits, and checked that the human disease papers were indeed patient reports or discovery cohorts. The evidence supports a single discovery line beginning with the 2025 preprint and extending into the 2026 JCI cohort plus later case reports.
- [h9] BORCS5 patient papers are dispersed under alternate clinical diagnoses and phenotype labels, including neuroaxonal dystrophy with osteopetrosis and nonspecific rare neurodevelopmental disorder, so comprehensive retrieval requires alias-based searching beyond the canonical NDOABA2 name.  (tested, region `Alternate phenotype aliases`)
  - rationale: PubMed already retrieves distinct BORCS5 case reports using noncanonical labels, indicating the disease is indexed across several phenotype framings. This would be falsified if those hits were all duplicate dissemination of a single cohort or if no additional independent patient reports were found under alternate labels.
  - evidence: 2 supporting, 0 refuting
  - local test notes: Tested hypothesis h9 by checking whether BORCS5 patient papers appear under alternate phenotype labels beyond NDOABA2. system:
You decide what happens to each tested hypothesis next, from the evidence.

## Decisions

- `keep`: the claim stands as it is; it is carried forward without retesting.
- `refine`: the claim needs a changed clause, scope or mechanism; give the new `statement`. It is tested as a new hypothesis.
- `shelve`: set it aside. It can be revived later if the run stops making progress.

## How to decide

- A result that rests on one measurement of one artifact is weak evidence either way.
- Do not shelve a claim that wins on some part of the task, even if it loses overall: say so in `rationale`.
- Weigh what supports each claim against what refutes it, and cite those observation ids in `rationale`.
- Decide every hypothesis listed. Call submit_revision once.
